newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong monetary boss vows to "burn" speculators.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong monetary boss vows to "burn" speculators.

text.p: Hong Kong monetary boss Joseph Yam has vowed to keep the Hong Kong and U.S. dollars pegged and to "burn" currency speculators with high interest rates.
The threat comes after a week of nervous trading in the Hong Kong dollar and a bout of selling on Friday. Traders have said renewed pressure was expected on the Hong Kong dollar this week.
But Yam, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive, said he was ready to take on any speculators and would punish them with crippling interest rates.
"Those banks involved in the speculation will suffer by paying a high interest rate to get the Hong Kong dollar funding to settle the deals," Yam told the South China Morning Post.

"We may charge them 12 percent or even 60 percent. The speculators will find that the funding cost for them to buy the Hong Kong dollar to settle their deals is far more than they earn from the exchange rate," he added.
"The speculators who sell short the Hong Kong dollar will get burned and will leave the Hong Kong market," Yam said.
A spokesman in Yam's office confirmed the remarks, saying they were made on Sunday.
The spokesman said the percentages were less important than the underlying message: Hong Kong will impose whatever interest rates that are necessary to thwart speculators.
The Hong Kong currency has been pegged at HK$7.8 per U.S. dollar since 1983.
During the recent currency turmoil in Asia, the Hong Kong dollar has stayed on the strong side of its unofficial one percent trading band, rarely straying from HK$7.75 to the U.S. dollar.
In thin Monday trade, the Hong Kong dollar was quoted at 7.7435/55 per U.S. dollar, compared to HK$7.7490/7.7500 on Friday. Monday is a public holiday in Hong Kong.
Local currency pegs to the U.S. dollar have snapped across Asia since early July, leading to effective devaluations of the Thai baht, Malaysian ringgit, Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso.
But Yam ruled out changing the Hong Kong-U.S. dollar peg and said the local currency would not be a target for a sustained speculative attack.
He said: "Unlike other Asian countries, Hong Kong's economic fundamentals are very good and we have large reserves to defend our currency."
Economists agree that the Hong Kong dollar would be a tough target for speculators, saying they believe it is fairly valued and noting the monetary authority has the means to defend it.
China could also be counted on to contribute some of its more than US$120 billion in foreign exchange reserves to a Hong Kong dollar defence.
That, along with Hong Kong's own reserves of around US$66 billion, would make an impressive fund to fight speculators.

Britain handed back Hong Kong to China on July 1 after more than 150 years of colonial rule. Economists have said Beijing would see a sustained speculative attack on the Hong Kong dollar as a direct attack on its own national interests.
"We would like to let the speculators know we have no need and no intention to change our currency policies," Yam said. -- Hong Kong Newsroom, (852) 2843-6441
